panels.figure_caption: CT imaging of pulmonary changes in a 32-Week pregnant patient with fulminant paraquat poisoning. (A) Chest CT on Day 3: Symmetric chest with increased lung markings and pleural thickening, without significant infiltrative lesions. (B) Chest CT on Day 5: Symmetric chest with increased lung markings, consolidation in the right middle lobe with “air bronchogram” sign, and exudative lesions in the left lower lobe. This image corresponds to the progression of pulmonary injury during the acute phase of PQ poisoning, with early signs of respiratory failure and organ dysfunction.
in_text_mentions: On Day 3, the chest CT revealed a symmetric chest with increased lung markings and pleural thickening. No significant infiltrative lesions were observed (Figure 2A). These findings are consistent with the early stage of PQ poisoning, where the lung changes are primarily related to inflammatory response and initial pulmonary injury, without clear signs of consolidation or infiltrative pathology.

Follow-up chest CT imaging demonstrated a progressive deterioration in pulmonary status, with: (1) increased pulmonary markings. (2) consolidative lesions in the right middle lobe, exhibiting an air bronchogram pattern. (3) exudative changes in the left lower lobe, indicative of ongoing inflammatory or infectious processes (Figure 2B).

in_text_mentions: the second day, her condition deteriorated. She was icteric (Fig. 1), developed shortness of breath, and had multiple ulcers over the dorsum of the tongue, characteristic of a “paraquat tongue” (Fig. 2). Laboratory test results of RFT and LFT reports revealed drastic elevations in the serum urea, creatinine, bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (Tables 1 and 2). Our patient had now developed acute kidney injury and hepatitis. Chest radiograph revealed findings of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).Figure 1.Icterus depicted on the sclera
